title: Inheritance
description: Let one class build on another instead of copying its code.

content.value: Imagine you write a `Dog` class and then a `Cat` class. Both store a name, both eat, both sleep. You would be copying the same three methods into every animal you add, and fixing a bug in `eat` would mean fixing it in every copy.

Inheritance is the way out. You write the shared parts once in a parent class, and each child class says which parent it builds on. The child starts out with everything the parent has, and then adds whatever makes it different.
The parent's name goes in parentheses after the child's name. `Dog` has no `__init__` and no `eat` of its own, and it does not need them: both came from `Animal`.

A `Dog` object is built exactly like any other object, and the parent's `__init__` runs to store the name. From then on you can call the parent's methods and the child's own methods on it, and there is nothing to tell them apart at the call.

buddy = Dog("Buddy")

buddy.eat()     # Buddy is eating!   (borrowed from Animal)
buddy.fetch()   # Buddy brings the ball back!   (Dog's own)

When you call a method, Python looks in the child class first. If it is not there, it looks at the parent. Press the buttons below to watch that search happen, and notice which box lights up each time.

Sometimes the parent's version is not right for a particular child. Because Python checks the child first, you can simply write a method with the same name in the child, and that one wins. This is called overriding.
Switch the override on in the widget above and call `speak()` again. The same call now lands in the child instead of the parent, and the parent's version is never reached.
`pass` is Python's way of saying there is deliberately nothing here. `Cow` inherits everything and adds nothing, and the body of a class or function is never allowed to be empty.

practice.question: Make a Dog called 'rover' and call its eat() method, which Dog inherits from Animal.
Give Cat its own speak() method that prints a meow, so it overrides the one from Animal.

quiz.question: What does a child class get through inheritance?
options: It gets the parent's attributes and methods
It gets a copy that never updates
quiz.explain: The child starts with everything the parent has and can then add its own, without any of the parent's code being copied.

quiz.question: How do you define a class 'Car' that inherits from 'Vehicle'?
quiz.explain: The parent's name goes in parentheses after the child's. Writing it the other way round would make Vehicle the child.

quiz.question: Both Animal and Dog define speak(). Which one runs for a Dog object?
options: Dog's, because Python checks the child class first
Animal's, because the parent always wins
Both of them, one after the other
quiz.explain: Python searches the child first and stops as soon as it finds the method. That is what makes overriding possible.
